headline: Wamphassuc Rocks at First Light: Bass Sliding Deep, Sea Bass Holding the Day Shift
subhead: The boulder fields are still producing, but the stripers have gone nocturnal and the albie watch is just starting to get interesting.
body_markdown:
There's a window right at first light, before the sun gets up over Fishers Island, when the boulder fields off Wamphassuc Point go quiet in a way that tells you something. No nervous water, no terns working — just the low hum of current moving through the rocks. I poled the skiff through there Tuesday morning and watched a school of peanut bunker pour off the ledge in a tight silver rope, no predators pushing them, just moving with the tide. That's the tell right now. The bait's here. The bass aren't up chasing it in daylight anymore.

Water's been sitting in that low-to-mid 70s band across the western Sound — Kings Point up near 71, New London running a touch cooler at 69.4 — and that gradient matters more than people think. The cooler water east of us is why Fishers Island Sound still fishes better in daylight than the water off New Haven or the Norwalk Islands, but even here the stripers have pushed down into the deep holes around Ram Island and gone to feeding mostly after dark or in that gray hour before sunrise. We called this coming — said last week the striper bite here was tied directly to tide strength coming out of neap, and sure enough, as the current's built back up this week, the fish have gotten more predictable, just not necessarily more visible. You want them, you're fishing the breakwater rocks and the Ram Island boulder field on the last two hours of the outgoing, at night, swimming a 3-inch olive-over-white Deceiver or a soft-bodied eel through the current seams where the rock drops into deeper water. Light tackle guys doing well with 1-ounce bucktails, white or chartreuse, bounced slow off the bottom on the drift — not ripped, just walked down along the ledges where the boulders stack up eight to fifteen feet.

Daytime, the more honest bite right now is fluke and sea bass, and that's been steady rather than spectacular — which is fine, that's what August gives you here. Sandy pockets between the boulder patches off Ram Island and the flats inside Little Narragansett Bay have been holding keeper fluke mixed with plenty of shorts, standard Sound pattern this time of year. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the incoming, has been the most consistent combo — you're covering ground over that mixed bottom, letting the jig tick the sand and pop up over the rock edges. Depths between 15 and 25 feet off the eastern side of Fishers Island have given up the better-grade fish, four and five pounds mixed in with the dinks.

Sea bass and porgy are the dependable structure bite right now, and I mean dependable — every trip out to the reef pile off Wamphassuc or the rocks tight to Ram Island, squid strips on a high-low rig, and you're into fish inside the first ten minutes. Nothing glamorous, but it's honest fishing, and it fills a cooler when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Blackfish season's closed through this stretch, so I'm scouting those same rocks for the fall reopener rather than fishing them — and there's plenty of tog sign around the breakwater boulders and out toward Wicopesset, which is good news for October.

Now the part everybody's actually asking me about at the dock — albies and bonito. Nothing yet. I want to be straight about that. We're watching Watch Hill Reef, Napatree Point, and the rip off East Point every morning for that first nervous water, the diving terns, the small dark backs breaking the surface — and it isn't there. The water's warm enough, temps at Montauk and Block Island have crossed the threshold that usually kicks this off, but the tidal push hasn't built enough yet to concentrate bait the way it needs to. The new moon on the 12th is the date I've got circled. Building current into that moon, especially on the outgoing at Napatree and around the tip of Fishers, is when I'd expect the first scout fish to show — small pods, here one tide and gone the next, before the real run fills in. If I had to bet, I'd say we're seven to ten days out from the first real sign, not longer.

What I'd do this week: fish the rocks at night for bass if you want a shot at a real fish, keep it honest with fluke and sea bass in daylight because that bite's not going anywhere, and start checking the reef edges at Watch Hill and Napatree every dawn from here on out with a bag of epoxy jigs and a 7-weight rigged and ready. When the albies show, they don't give you much notice, and around here the guys who catch the first wave are the ones who were already looking.
